steps.observation: Work on this for 30 seconds; do not stop early. Write a short story about a lighthouse keeper.

steps.action:
Way out on the ragged edge of Greywater Coast stood the Solace Point Lighthouse, a white-washed tower whose lantern had pierced sea-fog for more than a century. Its keeper, Rowan Hale, rose before dawn every day, his boots echoing on the spiral stair as gulls screeched overhead. He tested the brass oil valves, polished the Fresnel lens until it shone like trapped starlight, and wound the clockwork that turned the beacon. Though satellite navigation had long since charted every reef, Rowan believed ships still trusted the steady rhythm of a living light more than any blinking pixel on a screen.

One stormy October evening, a siren howled across the radio—distress from the fishing trawler Moira Lee, battered and powerless somewhere off Blackfang Shoal. Rowan’s pulse thrummed. He aligned the reflector to widen the beam, then dashed to the signal house, firing a flare skyward: a crimson arc against roiling clouds. Next he lowered an old lifeboat, half-expecting the coast guard to arrive first. They did not.

Rowan rowed hard, muscles burning, guided only by the lighthouse’s glow now shrinking behind him. Lightning forked, revealing the trawler listing like a wounded beast. He threw a grappling line, hauled himself aboard, and found the crew huddled beside a sputtering emergency lamp. Water flooded the hold. “She’ll sink if we stay,” Rowan shouted over the gale. With practiced calm, he ushered them into the lifeboat—six fishermen, cold but alive—and together they carved a wobbling path back toward the lighthouse’s ever-constant eye.

When dawn finally blushed across the horizon, the storm had spent its wrath. From the lantern room Rowan watched the rescued men trudge up the cliff track, grateful and wide-eyed, backlit by first light. Solace Point’s beacon winked off as the sun rose, duty done. Rowan set down his logbook, sipped black coffee, and smiled at the quiet keeper’s truth: some lights exist not just to warn of danger, but to remind those at sea—and on shore—that someone is always awake, watching the darkness so others may sleep.
